L22: ## 19.1 Heart Anatomy
L23: ### Learning Objectives
L24: 
L25: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
L26:   * Describe the location and position of the heart within the body cavity
L27:   * Describe the internal and external anatomy of the heart
L28:   * Identify the tissue layers of the heart
L29:   * Relate the structure of the heart to its function as a pump
L30:   * Compare systemic circulation to pulmonary circulation
L31:   * Identify the veins and arteries of the coronary circulation system
L32:   * Trace the pathway of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood thorough the chambers of the heart
L33: The vital importance of the heart is obvious. If one assumes an average rate of contraction of 75 contractions per minute, a human heart would contract approximately 108,000 times in one day, more than 39 million times in one year, and nearly 3 billion times during a 75-year lifespan. Each of the major pumping chambers of the heart ejects approximately 70 mL blood per contraction in a resting adult. This would be equal to 5.25 liters of fluid per minute and approximately 14,000 liters per day.
L34: Over one year, that would equal 10,000,000 liters or 2.6 million gallons of blood sent through roughly 60,000 miles of vessels. In order to understand how that happens, it is necessary to understand the anatomy and physiology of the heart.
L35: ### Location of the Heart
L36: The human heart is located within the thoracic cavity, medially between the lungs in the space known as the mediastinum. 【4†Figure 19.2】 shows the position of the heart within the thoracic cavity. Within the mediastinum, the heart is separated from the other mediastinal structures by a tough membrane known as the pericardium, or pericardial sac, and sits in its own space called the pericardial cavity.
L37: The dorsal surface of the heart lies near the bodies of the vertebrae, and its anterior surface sits deep to the sternum and costal cartilages. The great veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae, and the great arteries, the aorta and pulmonary trunk, are attached to the superior surface of the heart, called the base. The base of the heart is located at the level of the third costal cartilage, as seen in 【4†Figure 19.2】.
L38: The inferior tip of the heart, the apex, lies just to the left of the sternum between the junction of the fourth and fifth ribs near their articulation with the costal cartilages. The right side of the heart is deflected anteriorly, and the left side is deflected posteriorly. It is important to remember the position and orientation of the heart when placing a stethoscope on the chest of a patient and listening for heart sounds, and also when looking at images taken from a midsagittal perspective.
L39: The slight deviation of the apex to the left is reflected in a depression in the medial surface of the superior lobe of the left lung, called the cardiac notch.
L40: 【5†Image: This diagram shows the location of the heart in the thorax.】 Figure 19.2 Position of the Heart in the Thorax The heart is located within the thoracic cavity, medially between the lungs in the mediastinum. It is about the size of a fist, is broad at the top (called the base), and tapers toward the apex.
L41: ### Everyday Connection
L42: #### CPR
L43: The position of the heart in the torso between the vertebrae and sternum (see 【4†Figure 19.2】 for the position of the heart within the thorax) allows for individuals to apply an emergency technique known as cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) if the heart of a patient should stop.
L44: By applying pressure with the flat portion of one hand on the sternum in the area between the line at T4 and T9 (【6†Figure 19.3】), it is possible to manually compress the blood within the heart enough to push some of the blood within it into the pulmonary and systemic circuits. This is particularly critical for the brain, as irreversible damage and death of neurons occur within minutes of loss of blood flow.
L45: Current standards call for compression of the chest at least 5 cm deep and at a rate of 100 compressions per minute, a rate equal to the beat in “Staying Alive,” recorded in 1977 by the Bee Gees. If you are unfamiliar with this song, a version is available on 【7†www.youtube.com†www.youtube.com】. At this stage, the emphasis is on performing high-quality chest compressions, rather than providing artificial respiration.
L46: CPR is generally performed until the patient regains spontaneous contraction or is declared dead by an experienced healthcare professional.
L47: When performed by untrained or overzealous individuals, CPR can result in broken ribs or a broken sternum, and can inflict additional severe damage on the patient. It is also possible, if the hands are placed too low on the sternum, to manually drive the xiphoid process into the liver, a consequence that may prove fatal for the patient. Proper training is essential.
L48: This proven life-sustaining technique is so valuable that virtually all medical personnel as well as concerned members of the public should be certified and routinely recertified in its application. CPR courses are offered at a variety of locations, including colleges, hospitals, the American Red Cross, and some commercial companies. They normally include practice of the compression technique on a mannequin.
L49: 【8†Image: The top panel shows a schematic of a person performing CPR and demarcates the region in the chest where the compression must be performed. The bottom panel shows a photo of a person performing CPR on a dummy.】 Figure 19.3 CPR Technique If the heart should stop, CPR can maintain the flow of blood until the heart resumes beating. By applying pressure to the sternum, the blood within the heart will be squeezed out of the heart and into the circulation.
L50: Proper positioning of the hands on the sternum to perform CPR would be between the lines at T4 and T9.
L51: ### Interactive Link
L52: 
L53: Visit the American Heart Association 【9†website】 to help locate a course near your home in the United States. There are also many other national and regional heart associations that offer the same service, depending upon the location.
L54: ### Shape and Size of the Heart
L55: The shape of the heart is similar to a pinecone, rather broad at the superior surface and tapering to the apex (see 【4†Figure 19.2】). A typical heart is approximately the size of your fist: 12 cm (5 in) in length, 8 cm (3.5 in) wide, and 6 cm (2.5 in) in thickness. Given the size difference between most members of the sexes, the weight of a female heart is approximately 250–300 grams (9 to 11 ounces), and the weight of a male heart is approximately 300–350 grams (11 to 12 ounces).
L56: The heart of a well-trained athlete, especially one specializing in aerobic sports, can be considerably larger than this. Cardiac muscle responds to exercise in a manner similar to that of skeletal muscle. That is, exercise results in the addition of protein myofilaments that increase the size of the individual cells without increasing their numbers, a concept called hypertrophy. Hearts of athletes can pump blood more effectively at lower rates than those of nonathletes.
L57: Enlarged hearts are not always a result of exercise; they can result from pathologies, such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The cause of an abnormally enlarged heart muscle is unknown, but the condition is often undiagnosed and can cause sudden death in apparently otherwise healthy young people.
L58: ### Chambers and Circulation through the Heart
L59: 
L60: The human heart consists of four chambers: The left side and the right side each have one atrium and one ventricle. Each of the upper chambers, the right atrium (plural = atria) and the left atrium, acts as a receiving chamber and contracts to push blood into the lower chambers, the right ventricle and the left ventricle. The ventricles serve as the primary pumping chambers of the heart, propelling blood to the lungs or to the rest of the body.
L61: There are two distinct but linked circuits in the human circulation called the pulmonary and systemic circuits. Although both circuits transport blood and everything it carries, we can initially view the circuits from the point of view of gases. The pulmonary circuit transports blood to and from the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and delivers carbon dioxide for exhalation.
L62: The systemic circuit transports oxygenated blood to virtually all of the tissues of the body and returns relatively deoxygenated blood and carbon dioxide to the heart to be sent back to the pulmonary circulation.
L63: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk, which leads toward the lungs and bifurcates into the left and right pulmonary arteries. These vessels in turn branch many times before reaching the pulmonary capillaries, where gas exchange occurs: Carbon dioxide exits the blood and oxygen enters. The pulmonary trunk arteries and their branches are the only arteries in the post-natal body that carry relatively deoxygenated blood.
L64: Highly oxygenated blood returning from the pulmonary capillaries in the lungs passes through a series of vessels that join together to form the pulmonary veins—the only post-natal veins in the body that carry highly oxygenated blood. The pulmonary veins conduct blood into the left atrium, which pumps the blood into the left ventricle, which in turn pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and on to the many branches of the systemic circuit.
L65: Eventually, these vessels will lead to the systemic capillaries, where exchange with the tissue fluid and cells of the body occurs. In this case, oxygen and nutrients exit the systemic capillaries to be used by the cells in their metabolic processes, and carbon dioxide and waste products will enter the blood.
L66: The blood exiting the systemic capillaries is lower in oxygen concentration than when it entered. The capillaries will ultimately unite to form venules, joining to form ever-larger veins, eventually flowing into the two major systemic veins, the superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava, which return blood to the right atrium. The blood in the superior and inferior venae cavae flows into the right atrium, which pumps blood into the right ventricle.
L67: This process of blood circulation continues as long as the individual remains alive. Understanding the flow of blood through the pulmonary and systemic circuits is critical to all health professions (【10†Figure 19.4】).
L68: 【11†Image: The top panel shows the human heart with the arteries and veins labeled. The bottom panel shows the human circulatory system.】 Figure 19.4 Dual System of the Human Blood Circulation Blood flows from the right atrium to the right ventricle, where it is pumped into the pulmonary circuit. The blood in the pulmonary artery branches is low in oxygen but relatively high in carbon dioxide.
L69: Gas exchange occurs in the pulmonary capillaries (oxygen into the blood, carbon dioxide out), and blood high in oxygen and low in carbon dioxide is returned to the left atrium. From here, blood enters the left ventricle, which pumps it into the systemic circuit. Following exchange in the systemic capillaries (oxygen and nutrients out of the capillaries and carbon dioxide and wastes in), blood returns to the right atrium and the cycle is repeated.
L70: ### Membranes, Surface Features, and Layers
L71: 
L72: Our exploration of more in-depth heart structures begins by examining the membrane that surrounds the heart, the prominent surface features of the heart, and the layers that form the wall of the heart. Each of these components plays its own unique role in terms of function.
L73: #### Membranes
L74: The membrane that directly surrounds the heart and defines the pericardial cavity is called the pericardium or pericardial sac. It also surrounds the “roots” of the major vessels, or the areas of closest proximity to the heart. The pericardium, which literally translates as “around the heart,” consists of two distinct sublayers: the sturdy outer fibrous pericardium and the inner serous pericardium.
L75: The fibrous pericardium is made of tough, dense connective tissue that protects the heart and maintains its position in the thorax. The more delicate serous pericardium consists of two layers: the parietal pericardium, which is fused to the fibrous pericardium, and an inner visceral pericardium, or epicardium, which is fused to the heart and is part of the heart wall. The pericardial cavity, filled with lubricating serous fluid, lies between the epicardium and the pericardium.
L76: In most organs within the body, visceral serous membranes such as the epicardium are microscopic. However, in the case of the heart, it is not a microscopic layer but rather a macroscopic layer, consisting of a simple squamous epithelium called a mesothelium, reinforced with loose, irregular, or areolar connective tissue that attaches to the pericardium. This mesothelium secretes the lubricating serous fluid that fills the pericardial cavity and reduces friction as the heart contracts.
L77: 【12†Figure 19.5】 illustrates the pericardial membrane …2259 tokens truncated…les into the pulmonary trunk and aorta. Located in each of these openings between the atria and ventricles is a valve, a specialized structure that ensures one-way flow of blood. The valves between the atria and ventricles are known generically as atrioventricular valves.
L110: The valves at the openings that lead to the pulmonary trunk and aorta are known generically as semilunar valves. The interventricular septum is visible in 【20†Figure 19.9】. In this figure, the atrioventricular septum has been removed to better show the bicuspid and tricuspid valves; the interatrial septum is not visible, since its location is covered by the aorta and pulmonary trunk.
L111: Since these openings and valves structurally weaken the atrioventricular septum, the remaining tissue is heavily reinforced with dense connective tissue called the cardiac skeleton, or skeleton of the heart. It includes four rings that surround the openings between the atria and ventricles, and the openings to the pulmonary trunk and aorta, and serve as the point of attachment for the heart valves. The cardiac skeleton also provides an important boundary in the heart electrical conduction system.
L112: 【21†Image: In this figure the top panel shows the image of the heart with the major parts labeled. The bottom left panel shows a photo of the heart with the surface layer peeled off. The images on the bottom right show detailed musculature inside the heart.】 Figure 19.9 Internal Structures of the Heart This anterior view of the heart shows the four chambers, the major vessels and their early branches, as well as the valves.
L113: The presence of the pulmonary trunk and aorta covers the interatrial septum, and the atrioventricular septum is cut away to show the atrioventricular valves.
L114: ### Disorders of the...
L115: #### Heart: Heart Defects
L116: One very common form of interatrial septum pathology is patent foramen ovale, which occurs when the septum primum does not close at birth, and the fossa ovalis is unable to fuse. The word patent is from the Latin root patens for “open.” It may be benign or asymptomatic, perhaps never being diagnosed, or in extreme cases, it may require surgical repair to close the opening permanently.
L117: As much as 20–25 percent of the general population may have a patent foramen ovale, but fortunately, most have the benign, asymptomatic version. Patent foramen ovale is normally detected by auscultation of a heart murmur (an abnormal heart sound) and confirmed by imaging with an echocardiogram. Despite its prevalence in the general population, the causes of patent ovale are unknown, and there are no known risk factors.
L118: In nonlife-threatening cases, it is better to monitor the condition than to risk heart surgery to repair and seal the opening.
L119: Coarctation of the aorta is a congenital abnormal narrowing of the aorta that is normally located at the insertion of the ligamentum arteriosum, the remnant of the fetal shunt called the ductus arteriosus. If severe, this condition drastically restricts blood flow through the primary systemic artery, which is life threatening. In some individuals, the condition may be fairly benign and not detected until later in life.
L120: Detectable symptoms in an infant include difficulty breathing, poor appetite, trouble feeding, or failure to thrive. In older individuals, symptoms include dizziness, fainting, shortness of breath, chest pain, fatigue, headache, and nosebleeds. Treatment involves surgery to resect (remove) the affected region or angioplasty to open the abnormally narrow passageway. Studies have shown that the earlier the surgery is performed, the better the chance of survival.
L121: A patent ductus arteriosus is a congenital condition in which the ductus arteriosus fails to close. The condition may range from severe to benign. Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close results in blood flowing from the higher pressure aorta into the lower pressure pulmonary trunk. This additional fluid moving toward the lungs increases pulmonary pressure and makes respiration difficult.
L122: Symptoms include shortness of breath (dyspnea), tachycardia, enlarged heart, a widened pulse pressure, and poor weight gain in infants. Treatments include surgical closure (ligation), manual closure using platinum coils or specialized mesh inserted via the femoral artery or vein, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to block the synthesis of prostaglandin E2, which maintains the vessel in an open position. If untreated, the condition can result in congestive heart failure.
L123: Septal defects are not uncommon in individuals and may be congenital or caused by various disease processes. Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital condition that may also occur from exposure to unknown environmental factors; it occurs when there is an opening in the interventricular septum caused by blockage of the pulmonary trunk, normally at the pulmonary semilunar valve.
L124: This allows blood that is relatively low in oxygen from the right ventricle to flow into the left ventricle and mix with the blood that is relatively high in oxygen. Symptoms include a distinct heart murmur, low blood oxygen percent saturation, dyspnea or difficulty in breathing, polycythemia, broadening (clubbing) of the fingers and toes, and in children, difficulty in feeding or failure to grow and develop. It is the most common cause of cyanosis following birth.
L125: The term “tetralogy” is derived from the four components of the condition, although only three may be present in an individual patient: pulmonary infundibular stenosis (rigidity of the pulmonary valve), overriding aorta (the aorta is shifted above both ventricles), ventricular septal defect (opening), and right ventricular hypertrophy (enlargement of the right ventricle). Other heart defects may also accompany this condition, which is typically confirmed by echocardiography imaging.
L126: Tetralogy of Fallot occurs in approximately 400 out of one million live births. Normal treatment involves extensive surgical repair, including the use of stents to redirect blood flow and replacement of valves and patches to repair the septal defect, but the condition has a relatively high mortality. Survival rates are currently 75 percent during the first year of life; 60 percent by 4 years of age; 30 percent by 10 years; and 5 percent by 40 years.
L127: In the case of severe septal defects, including both tetralogy of Fallot and patent foramen ovale, failure of the heart to develop properly can lead to a condition commonly known as a “blue baby.” Regardless of normal skin pigmentation, individuals with this condition have an insufficient supply of oxygenated blood, which leads to cyanosis, a blue or purple coloration of the skin, especially when active.
L128: Septal defects are commonly first detected through auscultation, listening to the chest using a stethoscope. In this case, instead of hearing normal heart sounds attributed to the flow of blood and closing of heart valves, unusual heart sounds may be detected. This is often followed by medical imaging to confirm or rule out a diagnosis. In many cases, treatment may not be needed. Some common congenital heart defects are illustrated in 【22†Figure 19.10】.
L129: 【23†Image: This diagram shows the structure of the heart with different congenital defects. The top left panel shows patent foramen ovale, the top right panel shows coarctation of the aorta, the bottom left panel shows patent ductus ateriosus and the bottom right shows tetralogy of fallot.】 Figure 19.10 Congenital Heart Defects (a) A patent foramen ovale defect is an abnormal opening in the interatrial septum, or more commonly, a failure of the foramen ovale to close.
L130: (b) Coarctation of the aorta is an abnormal narrowing of the aorta. (c) A patent ductus arteriosus is the failure of the ductus arteriosus to close. (d) Tetralogy of Fallot includes an abnormal opening in the interventricular septum.
L131: #### Right Atrium
L132: The right atrium serves as the receiving chamber for blood returning to the heart from the systemic circulation. The two major systemic veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae, and the large coronary vein called the coronary sinus that drains the heart myocardium empty into the right atrium. The superior vena cava drains blood from regions superior to the diaphragm: the head, neck, upper limbs, and the thoracic region. It empties into the superior and posterior portions of the right atrium.
L133: The inferior vena cava drains blood from areas inferior to the diaphragm: the lower limbs and abdominopelvic region of the body. It, too, empties into the posterior portion of the atria, but inferior to the opening of the superior vena cava. Immediately superior and slightly medial to the opening of the inferior vena cava on the posterior surface of the atrium is the opening of the coronary sinus. This thin-walled vessel drains most of the coronary veins that return systemic blood from the heart.
L134: The majority of the internal heart structures discussed in this and subsequent sections are illustrated in 【20†Figure 19.9】.
L135: While the bulk of the internal surface of the right atrium is smooth, the depression of the fossa ovalis is medial, and the anterior surface demonstrates prominent ridges of muscle called the pectinate muscles. The right auricle also has pectinate muscles. The left atrium does not have pectinate muscles except in the auricle.
L136: The atria receive venous blood on a nearly continuous basis, preventing venous flow from stopping while the ventricles are contracting. While most ventricular filling occurs while the atria are relaxed, they do demonstrate a contractile phase and actively pump blood into the ventricles just prior to ventricular contraction. The opening between the atrium and ventricle is guarded by the tricuspid valve.
L137: #### Right Ventricle
L138: The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve. Each flap of the valve is attached to strong strands of connective tissue, the chordae tendineae, literally “tendinous cords,” or sometimes more poetically referred to as “heart strings.” There are several chordae tendineae associated with each of the flaps. They are composed of approximately 80 percent collagenous fibers with the remainder consisting of elastic fibers and endothelium.
L139: They connect each of the flaps to a papillary muscle that extends from the inferior ventricular surface. There are three papillary muscles in the right ventricle, called the anterior, posterior, and septal muscles, which correspond to the three sections of the valves.
L140: When the myocardium of the ventricle contracts, pressure within the ventricular chamber rises. Blood, like any fluid, flows from higher pressure to lower pressure areas, in this case, toward the pulmonary trunk and the atrium. To prevent any potential backflow, the papillary muscles also contract, generating tension on the chordae tendineae. This prevents the flaps of the valves from being forced into the atria and regurgitation of the blood back into the atria during ventricular contraction.
L141: 【24†Figure 19.11】 shows papillary muscles and chordae tendineae attached to the tricuspid valve.
L142: 【25†Image: This photo shows the inside of the heart with the main muscles labeled.】 Figure 19.11 Chordae Tendineae and Papillary Muscles In this frontal section, you can see papillary muscles attached to the tricuspid valve on the right as well as the mitral valve on the left via chordae tendineae. (credit: modification of work by “PV KS”/flickr.com)
L143: The walls of the ventricle are lined with trabeculae carneae, ridges of cardiac muscle covered by endocardium. In addition to these muscular ridges, a band of cardiac muscle, also covered by endocardium, known as the moderator band (see 【20†Figure 19.9】) reinforces the thin walls of the right ventricle and plays a crucial role in cardiac conduction.
L144: It arises from the inferior portion of the interventricular septum and crosses the interior space of the right ventricle to connect with the inferior papillary muscle.
L145: When the right ventricle contracts, it ejects blood into the pulmonary trunk, which branches into the left and right pulmonary arteries that carry it to each lung. The superior surface of the right ventricle begins to taper as it approaches the pulmonary trunk. At the base of the pulmonary trunk is the pulmonary semilunar valve that prevents backflow from the pulmonary trunk.
L146: #### Left Atrium
L147: After exchange of gases in the pulmonary capillaries, blood returns to the left atrium high in oxygen via one of the four pulmonary veins. While the left atrium does not contain pectinate muscles, it does have an auricle that includes these pectinate ridges. Blood flows nearly continuously from the pulmonary veins back into the atrium, which acts as the receiving chamber, and from here through an opening into the left ventricle.
L148: Most blood flows passively into the heart while both the atria and ventricles are relaxed, but toward the end of the ventricular relaxation period, the left atrium will contract, pumping blood into the ventricle. This atrial contraction accounts for approximately 20 percent of ventricular filling. The opening between the left atrium and ventricle is guarded by the mitral valve.
L149: #### Left Ventricle
L150: 
L151: Recall that, although both sides of the heart will pump the same amount of blood, the muscular layer is much thicker in the left ventricle compared to the right (see 【18†Figure 19.8】). Like the right ventricle, the left also has trabeculae carneae, but there is no moderator band. The mitral valve is connected to papillary muscles via chordae tendineae. There are two papillary muscles on the left—the anterior and posterior—as opposed to three on the right.

# Редакторская памятка каталога

## Сложность

- `easy`: факт известен большинству взрослых либо широкой демографической/культурной группе без регулярного погружения в предмет; все четыре варианта правдоподобны и одной категории, поэтому незнающий всё равно должен подумать. Одна лишь известность среди игроков, болельщиков или другого тематического сообщества не делает вопрос easy.
- `medium`: человек, регулярно соприкасающийся с темой, скорее всего ответит, а человек вне темы в основном сможет только сузить выбор или угадать.
- `hard`: нужна точная деталь, углублённое знание или нетривиальный вывод. Хотя бы часть неверных вариантов должна исключаться логикой или знанием контекста; четыре неразличимых случайных имени не подходят.
- Уровень определяется аудиторией и требуемым знанием, а не длиной формулировки. Один feedback-голос — повод перечитать вопрос, но не автоматический перенос.
- При аудите прежних 50 вопросов тема не подгоняется под старую квоту: каждый вопрос получает абсолютный уровень по этим критериям. После аудита новые вопросы заполняют фактический дефицит темы до итоговых `40/40/20`.
- Калибровочные якоря: герой The Legend of Zelda — `medium`, потому что вне игровой аудитории ответ обычно угадывают; Портсмутский договор — `medium`, потому что это узнаваемая школьная деталь для знакомых с историей, а не экспертный `hard`.

## Формулировка и варианты

- Вопрос имеет один устойчивый во времени правильный ответ. Для меняющегося факта в вопросе указан год или период.
- Вопрос читается вслух вместе с каждым вариантом. Падеж, число, род и форма всех четырёх вариантов согласованы; допустимы самостоятельные именные подписи в именительном падеже, если они последовательно используются во всех вариантах.
- Варианты относятся к одной смысловой категории, сопоставимы по детализации и не выдают ответ длиной, регистром или пунктуацией.
- Не используются «всё перечисленное», шуточные варианты и очевидно невозможные сущности. Дистрактор должен быть связан с темой вопроса и иметь объяснимую причину, почему его можно спутать с ответом.
- В каждом пакете позиции правильного ответа распределяются равномерно; для темы из 100 вопросов целевой итог — `10/10/10/10` внутри каждого уровня easy и medium и `5/5/5/5` внутри hard.

## Справки и объяснение

- Каждый из четырёх вариантов имеет отдельную `note` длиной до 35 слов. Справка самостоятельна: она кратко говорит, что это за человек, место, термин, произведение, число или утверждение.
- Запрещены как отрицательные заглушки («правдоподобный вариант», «другой ответ», «не подходит»), так и пустые ярлыки категории («город или название», «имя писателя», «биологический объект или понятие», «термин из условия»). Повтор правильного explanation после такого ярлыка не делает справку содержательной.
- Справка о неверном варианте не должна приписывать ему свойство правильного ответа. Она сообщает отдельный проверяемый факт именно о дистракторе: например, «Рим — столица Италии», «орган состоит из тканей и выполняет определённую функцию», «тай-брейк определяет победителя сета при равном счёте».
- Для составного ложного утверждения справка называет конкретное перепутанное правило, объект или величину. Фраза «смешивает свойство или связь» без этих названий запрещена.
- Автоматическое описание сущности разрешено только после проверки смысла в этом вопросе. Одноимённые люди, города, произведения и страницы значений нельзя подставлять по совпадению строки: такая справка считается фактической ошибкой.
- Для новых пакетов предпочтителен проверенный тематический пул сущностей: каждый дистрактор сам служит правильным ответом в другом вопросе темы и получает оттуда краткий канонический факт. Смысл строки и падеж всё равно проверяются вручную; неоднозначные названия в такой пул не включаются.
- Основное `explanation` содержит 2–4 предложения и не более 70 слов: прямо называет правильный ответ, объясняет его и при необходимости показывает ключевое различие с дистракторами.

## Источники и проверка

- `source.url` ведёт на точную HTTPS-страницу, которая подтверждает именно заданный факт; страницы поиска и главные страницы без нужного материала не принимаются.
- Предпочтение: официальный владелец факта или нормативный документ, затем музей, университет, научная организация или профильная энциклопедия. Для изменчивых технических и правовых фактов используется актуальный первичный источник.
- `verifiedAt` — фактическая дата последней проверки страницы и утверждения.
- Автор проверяет источник, но пакет принимает другой reviewer. Reviewer повторно проверяет правильный ответ, сложность, четыре подстановки, справки, дистракторы, дубликаты и ссылку.

## Идентификаторы и дубликаты

- `topicId` и `questionId` используют kebab-case; прежние 1500 ID не меняются.
- Новый вопрос проверяется на совпадение факта и формулировки внутри темы и во всём каталоге. Перефразирование уже существующего вопроса не считается новым фактом.
- Тематические границы берутся из `taxonomy-manifest.json`; вопрос за пределами `scope` или внутри `antiOverlap` переносится в подходящую тему до review.
Каталог SHALL применять единые критерии трёх уровней. Easy SHALL проверять широко известный взрослой аудитории факт, включая знания, широко распространённые внутри большой демографической или культурной группы; medium SHALL быть вероятно решаем игроком, знакомым с конкретной тематикой, и существенно труднее для игрока вне неё; hard SHALL требовать специфического знания либо содержательной логики. Каждый вопрос MUST оставаться однозначным, а его неверные варианты MUST быть правдоподобными и позволять игроку без точного знания по возможности сузить выбор без явно абсурдных дистракторов.

#### Scenario: Новый easy-вопрос
- **WHEN** редактор проверяет easy-вопрос
- **THEN** большинство взрослых либо широкая релевантная группа может знать ответ без специальной подготовки, а игрок без знания видит несколько грамматически и смыслово допустимых вариантов

#### Scenario: Medium-вопрос
- **WHEN** редактор проверяет medium-вопрос
- **THEN** знакомый с темой игрок, скорее всего, узнаёт ответ, а игрок вне темы не получает его только из очевидной несостоятельности остальных вариантов

#### Scenario: Hard-вопрос
- **WHEN** редактор проверяет hard-вопрос
- **THEN** вопрос требует специфического знания или многошагового вывода, но его варианты содержат контекстные признаки для разумного исключения хотя бы части ответов в большинстве пакета
## Контент вопросов

- Каталог содержит не менее 100 тематик и минимум 100 вопросов в каждой; текущая ревизия включает 110 тематик, в том числе существующие 30 и десять отдельно выделенных страновых историй. Базовый пакет содержит 40 easy, 40 medium и 20 hard; тема с подтверждённым запасом независимых фактов и источников может содержать 200 вопросов с квотой 80/80/40 или 300 с квотой 120/120/60.
- Easy-вопрос проверяет широко известный взрослой аудитории факт, включая знания, распространённые внутри большой демографической или культурной группы. Он не строится на редких датах, терминологической ловушке или второстепенной детали, но его неверные варианты остаются правдоподобными и не выдают ответ абсурдностью.
- Medium-вопрос, скорее всего, решает человек, знакомый с конкретной тематикой; игрок вне темы не должен получать правильный вариант только через очевидную несостоятельность остальных.
- Hard-вопрос требует специфического знания или содержательной логики. В большинстве hard-пакета варианты дают возможность разумно сузить выбор даже без точного знания; вопросы с четырьмя неразличимыми догадками используются ограниченно.
- Все 1500 вопросов прежней ревизии сохраняют идентификаторы. Изменение уровня, грамматики или дистрактора фиксируется в воспроизводимом отчёте аудита с причиной.
- Каждый вопрос имеет четыре различных варианта, ровно один правильный ответ, основное объяснение и краткую справку для каждого варианта.
- Каждая справка относится к св…1256 tokens truncated…язь с названием и утверждённой областью темы. Совпадение отдельного слова, географическое упоминание или связь только в справке не заменяет эту проверку. Междисциплинарные вопросы допустимы при явной связи; спорные границы и отсутствие определённой области фиксируются для ручной калибровки. Для несоответствия сохраняются исходная тема, причина и предложение переноса, изменения формулировки или исключения; каталог меняется только в отдельно согласованном этапе. Для пилота одобрено направление переноса вопроса о годе запуска «Хаббла» из «Астрономия и космос» в «Космические полёты»; перед импортом проверяются квоты, источники, notes и повторы. Для вопроса с рекомендацией CDC о выборе напитка одобрен перенос из «Напитки мира» в «Человек и медицина» после проверки пригодности, границ целевой темы, источников, notes, квот и повторов; решение не подтверждает сам медицинский совет. Вопрос о гражданской науке остаётся в «Экология и окружающая среда» с уточнением участия добровольцев именно в мониторинге окружающей среды; точный текст и варианты проверяет редактор.
- Граница тем настольных и карточных игр: «Настольные игры» включают современные авторские настольные игры с картами (например, Love Letter), исключая шахматы, классические и коллекционные карточные игры и компьютерные игры. «Карточные игры» охватывают классические и коллекционные карточные игры, колоды, комбинации и историю; современные авторские настольные игры с картами относятся к теме настольных. При пересечении современного авторского и коллекционного признаков приоритет имеет категория коллекционных карточных игр. Love Letter остаётся в «Настольных играх». Обновление кодовой taxonomy и проверка затронутых карточек выполняются отдельным этапом; исходный snapshot пилота сохраняется.
- Первый пакет `question-quality-batch-1` реализует принятую рубрику максимум на 20 исходных карточках вместе с компенсациями уровней и тематик. Размеры тем, квоты уровней и баланс позиций ключа сохраняются. Исходная карточка про «расстегнуться» остаётся hold в evidence и удаляется из игрового каталога; слот занимает независимый проверенный факт, старый ключ не утверждается. Условный перенос CDC остаётся для следующего ограниченного пакета. Приёмка точной поставленной версии проводится общим итогом.
- Объяснение содержит от двух до четырёх предложений и ориентировочно не более 70 слов.
- Каждый вопрос содержит источник и дату фактологической проверки. Название источника и ссылка показываются после объяснения раскрытого ответа; дата проверки остаётся служебной. Вопросы о современной культуре используют явный временной контекст и не формулируются через меняющееся «на сегодняшний день».
- Вопрос и все четыре ответа проверяются как законченные конструкции или подстановки: падеж, число, род, управление, пунктуация и написание имён согласуются без грамматической подсказки к правильному варианту.
- Локальная история заданных вопросов переживает новые партии. Вопрос помечается использованным сразу при показе, независимо от ответа и последующего рестарта.
- Для каждой пары «тематика × сложность» используется отдельная сохраняемая shuffle-bag полного размера уровня: 40/40/20, 80/80/40 или 120/120/60 для easy/medium/hard. В рамках одного цикла каждый вопрос показывается ровно один раз в воспроизводимо перемешанном порядке.
- После исчерпания bag создаётся новая seeded-перестановка: она не должна полностью совпадать с предыдущей, а первый вопрос нового цикла не может быть последним вопросом предыдущего цикла.
- Внутри одной партии выбранные темы и вопросы исключаются из повторного выбора. Исключение для темы: если иначе невозможно соблюсти лимит групп, возвращается минимально необходимое число ранее выбранных тем с новыми доступными вопросами. Возвращение темы не сбрасывает историю сыгранных вопросов; существующие отдельные правила полного исчерпания вопросов сохраняются. Показанные, но не выбранные темы имеют пониженный приоритет.
- Каждая тема принадлежит одной из существующих 13 явных валидируемых областей taxonomy; эти области служат группами для выбора. Профиль разнообразия `topic-diversity-v1` применяется к solo, classic, network и финальному выбору: обычный и финальный набор — не более одной темы группы; бонусный набор из 3 тем — не более одной, из 4–5 тем — не более двух. При возможности группы всех карточек различаются; повтор группы в большом бонусе допустим только при нехватке разных доступных групп. Лимит относится к одному набору, а не к соседним вопросам. В одном наборе topicId уникален; равноприоритетные варианты воспроизводимы от seed. При истинном исчерпании лимит не ослабляется молча.
- История вопросов хранит только компактные сведения, необходимые для частоты и давности повторов, а не полные результаты прошлых партий.
- В настройках доступен отдельный сброс истории вопросов с явным подтверждением; сохранённая незавершённая партия этим действием не удаляется.
- Каждый вопрос имеет минимум один проверяемый авторитетный источник. После подготовки каждый пакет проходит отдельную редакторскую проверку другим агентом по фактологии, индексу ответа, уровню, дистракторам, справкам вариантов, русской грамматике и дублям до интеграции.
- Оценки assigned/perceived difficulty используются только как редакторский сигнал. Одиночный голос не переносит вопрос автоматически; отчёт показывает объём выборки и силу расхождения, а итоговый уровень всегда подтверждается ручным аудитом.

- Инициатива `catalog-question-quality` охватывает все 11 000 вопросов и 110 тем: общий поиск дефектов prompt/key/answer/note/explanation формирует проверяемую очередь точных и смысловых повторов, утечек ключа, пересекающихся ответов и несоответствия теме; автоматический scan не подтверждает фактическую истинность. Полная редактура проводится волнами по 5 тем / 500 вопросов с поштучной проверкой ключа, четырёх notes, explanation и содержательных passages реально прочитанных источников, затем независимой редакторской проверкой и отдельной поставкой. L22: ## 20.5 Circulatory Pathways
L23: ### Learning Objectives
L24: 
L25: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
L26:   * Identify the vessels through which blood travels within the pulmonary circuit, beginning from the right ventricle of the heart and ending at the left atrium
L27:   * Create a flow chart showing the major systemic arteries through which blood travels from the aorta and its major branches, to the most significant arteries feeding into the right and left upper and lower limbs
L28:   * Create a flow chart showing the major systemic veins through which blood travels from the feet to the right atrium of the heart
L29: Virtually every cell, tissue, organ, and system in the body is impacted by the circulatory system. This includes the generalized and more specialized functions of transport of materials, capillary exchange, maintaining health by transporting white blood cells and various immunoglobulins (antibodies), hemostasis, regulation of body temperature, and helping to maintain acid-base balance. In addition to these shared functions, many systems enjoy a unique relationship with the circulatory system.
L30: 【4†Figure 20.22】 summarizes these relationships.
L31: 【5†Image: This table outlines the role of the circulatory system in the other organ systems in the body.】 Figure 20.22 Interaction of the Circulatory System with Other Body Systems
L32: As you learn about the vessels of the systemic and pulmonary circuits, notice that many arteries and veins share the same names, parallel one another throughout the body, and are very similar on the right and left sides of the body. These pairs of vessels will be traced through only one side of the body. Where differences occur in branching patterns or when vessels are singular, this will be indicated.
L33: For example, you will find a pair of femoral arteries and a pair of femoral veins, with one vessel on each side of the body. In contrast, some vessels closer to the midline of the body, such as the aorta, are unique. Moreover, some superficial veins, such as the great saphenous vein in the femoral region, have no arterial counterpart. Another phenomenon that can make the study of vessels challenging is that names of vessels can change with location.
L34: Like a street that changes name as it passes through an intersection, an artery or vein can change names as it passes an anatomical landmark. For example, the left subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery as it passes through the body wall and into the axillary region, and then becomes the brachial artery as it flows from the axillary region into the upper arm (or brachium). You will also find examples of anastomoses where two blood vessels that previously branched reconnect.
L35: Anastomoses are especially common in veins, where they help maintain blood flow even when one vessel is blocked or narrowed, although there are some important ones in the arteries supplying the brain.
L36: As you read about circular pathways, notice that there is an occasional, very large artery referred to as a trunk, a term indicating that the vessel gives rise to several smaller arteries. For example, the celiac trunk gives rise to the left gastric, common hepatic, and splenic arteries.
L37: As you study this section, imagine you are on a “Voyage of Discovery” similar to Lewis and Clark’s expedition in 1804–1806, which followed rivers and streams through unfamiliar territory, seeking a water route from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean. You might envision being inside a miniature boat, exploring the various branches of the circulatory system. This simple approach has proven effective for many students in mastering these major circulatory patterns.
L38: Another approach that works well for many students is to create simple line drawings similar to the ones provided, labeling each of the major vessels. It is beyond the scope of this text to name every vessel in the body. However, we will attempt to discuss the major pathways for blood and acquaint you with the major named arteries and veins in the body. Also, please keep in mind that individual variations in circulation patterns are not uncommon.
L39: ### Interactive Link
L40: 
L41: Visit this 【6†site】 for a brief summary of the arteries.
L42: ### Pulmonary Circulation
L43: Recall that blood returning from the systemic circuit enters the right atrium (【7†Figure 20.23】) via the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus, which drains the blood supply of the heart muscle. These vessels will be described more fully later in this section.
L44: This blood is relatively low in oxygen and relatively high in carbon dioxide, since much of the oxygen has been extracted for use by the tissues and the waste gas carbon dioxide was picked up to be transported to the lungs for elimination. From the right atrium, blood moves into the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs for gas exchange. This system of vessels is referred to as the pulmonary circuit.
L45: The single vessel exiting the right ventricle is the pulmonary trunk. At the base of the pulmonary trunk is the pulmonary semilunar valve, which prevents backflow of blood into the right ventricle during ventricular diastole. As the pulmonary trunk reaches the superior surface of the heart, it curves posteriorly and rapidly bifurcates (divides) into two branches, a left and a right pulmonary artery.
L46: To prevent confusion between these vessels, it is important to refer to the vessel exiting the heart as the pulmonary trunk, rather than also calling it a pulmonary artery. The pulmonary arteries in turn branch many times within the lung, forming a series of smaller arteries and arterioles that eventually lead to the pulmonary capillaries. The pulmonary capillaries surround lung structures known as alveoli that are the sites of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.
L47: Once gas exchange is completed, oxygenated blood flows from the pulmonary capillaries into a series of pulmonary venules that eventually lead to a series of larger pulmonary veins. Four pulmonary veins, two on the left and two on the right, return blood to the left atrium. At this point, the pulmonary circuit is complete. 【8†Table 20.4】 defines the major arteries and veins of the pulmonary circuit discussed in the text.
L48: 【9†Image: This diagram shows the network of blood vessels in the lungs.】 Figure 20.23 Pulmonary Circuit Blood exiting from the right ventricle flows into the pulmonary trunk, which bifurcates into the two pulmonary arteries. These vessels branch to supply blood to the pulmonary capillaries, where gas exchange occurs within the lung alveoli. Blood returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

L58: ### Overview of Systemic Arteries
L59: 
L60: Blood relatively high in oxygen concentration is returned from the pulmonary circuit to the left atrium via the four pulmonary veins. From the left atrium, blood moves into the left ventricle, which pumps blood into the aorta. The aorta and its branches—the systemic arteries—send blood to virtually every organ of the body (【10†Figure 20.24】).
L61: 【11†Image: This diagrams shows the major arteries in the human body.】 Figure 20.24 Systemic Arteries The major systemic arteries shown here deliver oxygenated blood throughout the body.
L62: ### The Aorta
L63: The aorta is the largest artery in the body (【12†Figure 20.25】). It arises from the left ventricle and eventually descends to the abdominal region, where it bifurcates at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra into the two common iliac arteries. The aorta consists of the ascending aorta, the aortic arch, and the descending aorta, which passes through the diaphragm and a landmark that divides into the superior thoracic and inferior abdominal components.
L64: Arteries originating from the aorta ultimately distribute blood to virtually all tissues of the body. At the base of the aorta is the aortic semilunar valve that prevents backflow of blood into the left ventricle while the heart is relaxing. After exiting the heart, the ascending aorta moves in a superior direction for approximately 5 cm and ends at the sternal angle. Following this ascent, it reverses direction, forming a graceful arc to the left, called the aortic arch.
L65: The aortic arch descends toward the inferior portions of the body and ends at the level of the intervertebral disk between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae. Beyond this point, the descending aorta continues close to the bodies of the vertebrae and passes through an opening in the diaphragm known as the aortic hiatus. Superior to the diaphragm, the aorta is called the thoracic aorta, and inferior to the diaphragm, it is called the abdominal aorta.
L66: The abdominal aorta terminates when it bifurcates into the two common iliac arteries at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra. See 【12†Figure 20.25】 for an illustration of the ascending aorta, the aortic arch, and the initial segment of the descending aorta plus major branches; 【13†Table 20.5】 summarizes the structures of the aorta.
L67: 【14†Image: This diagram shows the aorta and the major parts are labeled.】 Figure 20.25 Aorta The aorta has distinct regions, including the ascending aorta, aortic arch, and the descending aorta, which includes the thoracic and abdominal regions.

L79: #### Coronary Circulation
L80: The first vessels that branch from the ascending aorta are the paired coronary arteries (see 【12†Figure 20.25】), which arise from two of the three sinuses in the ascending aorta just superior to the aortic semilunar valve. These sinuses contain the aortic baroreceptors and chemoreceptors critical to maintain cardiac function. The left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus. The right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus.
L81: Normally, the right posterior aortic sinus does not give rise to a vessel.
L82: The coronary arteries encircle the heart, forming a ring-like structure that divides into the next level of branches that supplies blood to the heart tissues. (Seek additional content for more detail on cardiac circulation.)
L83: #### Aortic Arch Branches
L84: 
L85: There are three major branches of the aortic arch: the brachiocephalic artery, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian (literally “under the clavicle”) artery. As you would expect based upon proximity to the heart, each of these vessels is classified as an elastic artery.
L86: The brachiocephalic artery is located only on the right side of the body; there is no corresponding artery on the left. The brachiocephalic artery branches into the right subclavian artery and the right common carotid artery. The left subclavian and left common carotid arteries arise independently from the aortic arch but otherwise follow a similar pattern and distribution to the corresponding arteries on the right side (see 【7†Figure 20.23】).
L87: Each subclavian artery supplies blood to the arms, chest, shoulders, back, and central nervous system. It then gives rise to three major branches: the internal thoracic artery, the vertebral artery, and the thyrocervical artery. The internal thoracic artery, or mammary artery, supplies blood to the thymus, the pericardium of the heart, and the anterior chest wall.
L88: The vertebral artery passes through the vertebral foramen in the cervical vertebrae and then through the foramen magnum into the cranial cavity to supply blood to the brain and spinal cord. The paired vertebral arteries join together to form the large basilar artery at the base of the medulla oblongata. This is an example of an anastomosis. The subclavian artery also gives rise to the thyrocervical artery that provides blood to the thyroid, the cervical region of the neck, and the upper back and shoulder.
L89: The common carotid artery divides into internal and external carotid arteries. The right common carotid artery arises from the brachiocephalic artery and the left common carotid artery arises directly from the aortic arch. The external carotid artery supplies blood to numerous structures within the face, lower jaw, neck, esophagus, and larynx. These branches include the lingual, facial, occipital, maxillary, and superficial temporal arteries.

L123: #### Thoracic Aorta and Major Branches
L124: The thoracic aorta begins at the level of vertebra T5 and continues through to the diaphragm at the level of T12, initially traveling within the mediastinum to the left of the vertebral column. As it passes through the thoracic region, the thoracic aorta gives rise to several branches, which are collectively referred to as visceral branches and parietal branches (【20†Figure 20.28】).
L125: Those branches that supply blood primarily to visceral organs are known as the visceral branches and include the bronchial arteries, pericardial arteries, esophageal arteries, and the mediastinal arteries, each named after the tissues it supplies. Each bronchial artery (typically two on the left and one on the right) supplies systemic blood to the lungs and visceral pleura, in addition to the blood pumped to the lungs for oxygenation via the pulmonary circuit.
L126: The bronchial arteries follow the same path as the respiratory branches, beginning with the bronchi and ending with the bronchioles. There is considerable, but not total, intermingling of the systemic and pulmonary blood at anastomoses in the smaller branches of the lungs.
L127: This may sound incongruous—that is, the mixing of systemic arterial blood high in oxygen with the pulmonary arterial blood lower in oxygen—but the systemic vessels also deliver nutrients to the lung tissue just as they do elsewhere in the body. The mixed blood drains into typical pulmonary veins, whereas the bronchial artery branches remain separate and drain into bronchial veins described later.
L128: Each pericardial artery supplies blood to the pericardium, the esophageal artery provides blood to the esophagus, and the mediastinal artery provides blood to the mediastinum. The remaining thoracic aorta branches are collectively referred to as parietal branches or somatic branches, and include the intercostal and superior phrenic arteries. Each intercostal artery provides blood to the muscles of the thoracic cavity and vertebral column.
L129: The superior phrenic artery provides blood to the superior surface of the diaphragm. 【21†Table 20.7】 lists the arteries of the thoracic region.

L144: #### Abdominal Aorta and Major Branches
L145: After crossing through the diaphragm at the aortic hiatus, the thoracic aorta is called the abdominal aorta (see 【20†Figure 20.28】). L51: This is a fact sheet intended for health professionals. For a general overview, see our 【22†consumer fact sheet】.
L52: ## Introduction
L53: Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble vitamin that is naturally present in some foods, added to others, and available as a dietary supplement and a prescription medication. Because vitamin B12 contains the mineral cobalt, compounds with vitamin B12 activity are collectively called cobalamins [【23†1】]. Methylcobalamin and 5-deoxyadenosylcobalamin are the metabolically active forms of vitamin B12.
L54: However, two others forms, hydroxycobalamin and cyanocobalamin, become biologically active after they are converted to methylcobalamin or 5-deoxyadenosylcobalamin [【23†1-3】].
L55: Vitamin B12 is required for the development, myelination, and function of the central nervous system; healthy red blood cell formation; and DNA synthesis [【23†1】,【24†4】,【25†5】]. Vitamin B12 functions as a cofactor for two enzymes, methionine synthase and L-methylmalonyl-CoA mutase [【23†1-3】,【25†5】]. Methionine synthase catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to the essential amino acid methionine [【23†1】,【26†2】].
L56: Methionine is required for the formation of S-adenosylmethionine, a universal methyl donor for almost 100 different substrates, including DNA, RNA, proteins, and lipids [【27†3】,【25†5】]. L-methylmalonyl-CoA mutase converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the metabolism of propionate, a short-chain fatty acid [【26†2】].
L57: Vitamin B12 is bound to protein in food and must be released before it is absorbed [【25†5】]. The process starts in the mouth when food is mixed with saliva. The freed vitamin B12 then binds with haptocorrin, a cobalamin-binding protein in the saliva. More vitamin B12 is released from its food matrix by the activity of hydrochloric acid and gastric protease in the stomach, where it then binds to haptocorrin [【23†1】].
L58: In the duodenum, digestive enzymes free the vitamin B12 from haptocorrin, and this freed vitamin B12 combines with intrinsic factor, a transport and delivery binding protein secreted by the stomach’s parietal cells. The resulting complex is absorbed in the distal ileum by receptor-mediated endocytosis [【23†1】,【25†5】]. If vitamin B12 is added to fortified foods and dietary supplements, it is already in free form and therefore does not require the separation step.
L59: ### Assessing Vitamin B12 Status
L60: 
L61: Serum or plasma vitamin B12 levels are typically used to assess a person’s vitamin B12 status, with values lower than 200 or 250 pg/mL generally being considered subnormal. The most sensitive marker of vitamin B12 status is a vitamin B12-associated metabolite called methylmalonic acid, and serum levels of this metabolite can be used to confirm a diagnosis of vitamin B12 deficiency if a patient’s serum vitamin B12 level is between 150 and 399 pg/mL.
L62: Vitamin B12 status is typically assessed by measurements of serum or plasma vitamin B12 levels. The cutoff between normal vitamin B12 levels and deficiency varies by method and laboratory, but most laboratories define subnormal serum or plasma values as those lower than 200 or 250 picograms per milliliter (pg/mL) (148 or 185 picomols per liter [pmol/L]) [【26†2】].
L63: Levels of serum methylmalonic acid (MMA), a vitamin B12-associated metabolite, are the most sensitive markers of vitamin B12 status, and an MMA level greater than 0.271 micromol/L suggests vitamin B12 deficiency [【28†6-8】]. However, MMA levels also rise with renal insufficiency and tend to be higher in older adults [【28†6】,【29†9】,【30†10】].
L64: Another marker is total plasma homocysteine levels, which rise quickly as vitamin B12 status declines; a serum homocysteine level higher than 15 micromol/L, for example, suggests vitamin B12 deficiency [【31†11】]. However, this indicator has poor specificity because it is influenced by other factors, such as low folate levels and, especially, by declines in kidney function [【28†6】].
L65: Experts suggest that if a patient’s serum vitamin B12 level is between 150 to 399 pg/mL (111 to 294 pmol/L), the patient’s serum MMA levels should be checked to help confirm a diagnosis of vitamin B12 deficiency [【32†7】,【29†9】].
L66: ## Recommended Intakes
L67: 
L68: The Food and Nutrition Board at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine has established Recommended Dietary Allowances and Adequate Intakes for vitamin B12. These values range from 2.4 to 2.8 mcg for adults and from 0.4 to 2.8 mcg for infants, children, and adolescents, depending on age.
L69: Intake recommendations for vitamin B12 and other nutrients are provided in the Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs) developed by the Food and Nutrition Board (FNB) at the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine [【23†1】]. DRI is the general term for a set of reference values used for planning and assessing nutrient intakes of healthy people. These values, which vary by age and sex, include the following:
L70:   * Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA): Average daily level of intake sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all (97%–98%) healthy individuals; often used to plan nutritionally adequate diets for individuals
L71:   * Adequate Intake (AI): Intake at this level is assumed to ensure nutritional adequacy; established when evidence is insufficient to develop an RDA
L72:   * Estimated Average Requirement (EAR): Average daily level of intake estimated to meet the requirements of 50% of healthy individuals; usually used to assess the nutrient intakes of groups of people and to plan nutritionally adequate diets for them; can also be used to assess the nutrient intakes of individuals
L73:   * Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL): Maximum daily intake unlikely to cause adverse health effects
L74: Table 1 lists the current RDAs for vitamin B12 [【23†1】]. For adults, the main criterion that the FNB used to establish the RDAs was the amount needed to maintain a healthy hematological status and serum vitamin B12 levels. For infants age 0 to 12 months, the FNB established an AI that is equivalent to the mean intake of vitamin B12 in healthy, breastfed infants.

L86: ## Sources of Vitamin B12
L87: ### Food
L88: 
L89: Vitamin B12 is found in foods of animal origin. It is not naturally present in plant foods, but some plant foods are fortified with vitamin B12, including many breakfast cereals and nutritional yeasts. Breast milk also contains a small amount of vitamin B12. The bioavailability of vitamin B12 from food varies by vitamin B12 dose and by the type of food source.
L90: 
L91: Vitamin B12 is present in foods of animal origin, including fish, meat, poultry, eggs, and dairy products [【25†5】,【33†12】].
L92: Plant foods do not naturally contain vitamin B12. However, fortified breakfast cereals and fortified nutritional yeasts are readily available sources of vitamin B12 that have high bioavailability [【34†13】,【35†14】].
L93: The average vitamin B12 level in the breast milk of women with vitamin B12 intakes above the RDA is 0.44 micrograms (mcg)/L [【36†15】]. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) specifies that infant formulas sold in the United States must provide at least 0.15 mcg vitamin B12 per 100 kcal [【37†16】].
L94: The estimated bioavailability of vitamin B12 from food varies by vitamin B12 dose because absorption decreases drastically when the capacity of intrinsic factor is exceeded (at 1–2 mcg of vitamin B12) [【38†17】]. Bioavailability also varies by type of food source.
L95: For example, the bioavailability of vitamin B12 appears to be about three times higher in dairy products than in meat, fish, and poultry, and the bioavailability of vitamin B12 from dietary supplements is about 50% higher than that from food sources [【39†18-20】].
